title: Voltage Can Reverse an Ion's Flow

scenes.tts: Which way does potassium flow? Take a cell with 140 millimolar potassium inside and 5 outside, and hold it at minus 70 millivolts. Open the channels, and potassium leaves. Hold it at minus 100 millivolts, and potassium comes in, against a 28-fold concentration difference. Only the voltage changed.
scenes.visual: Cell wall with two K+ channels; ions inside and outside; voltage ruler. At -70 mV ions exit, then at -100 mV the case resets and ions enter.
scenes.narration: Which way does potassium flow? Take a cell with 140 millimolar potassium inside and 5 outside, and hold it at minus 70 millivolts. Open the channels, and potassium leaves. Hold it at minus 100 millivolts, and potassium comes in, against a 28-fold concentration difference. Only the voltage changed.

scenes.tts: An ion feels two pushes. One is its concentration difference. The other is the membrane potential, the inside minus the outside, and a negative one pulls cations in. For each ion, one voltage balances the two pushes, and that is its equilibrium potential. Ions still cross there, in equal numbers each way.
scenes.visual: One enlarged channel with a K+ ion; an orange arrow outward (concentration) and a teal arrow inward (voltage) that shrinks to match; ions then cross up and down, net flux zero.
scenes.narration: An ion feels two pushes. One is its concentration difference. The other is the membrane potential, the inside minus the outside, and a negative one pulls cations in. For each ion, one voltage balances the two pushes, and that is its equilibrium potential. Ions still cross there, in equal numbers each way.

scenes.tts: The Nernst equation gives that voltage. It takes the charge, the temperature, and the ratio of outside to inside concentration. These are teaching values, close to those of a typical mammalian cell. For potassium at 37 degrees Celsius, that ratio is 5 over 140, and its natural log is minus 3.33. Multiply by 26.7 millivolts, and the equilibrium potential for potassium is minus 89.1 millivolts.
scenes.visual: The equation is written, filled in for potassium line by line, and the result drops onto the voltage ruler as a green mark at -89.1 mV.
scenes.narration: The Nernst equation gives that voltage. It takes the charge, the temperature, and the ratio of outside to inside concentration. scenes.tts: Now compare each voltage with that potassium potential. At minus 70, the difference is plus 19.1 millivolts. Moving potassium in is uphill, so net flow is outward. At minus 100, the difference is minus 10.9 millivolts. Moving potassium in is now downhill, so net flow is inward, and the voltage outweighs the concentration.
scenes.visual: Ruler with the green E_K mark; the teal Vm mark sits at -70 then moves to -100 with the gap, uphill or downhill label and the net flux arrow reset and redrawn for each case.

scenes.tts: The same difference sets the current through one channel. Suppose a potassium channel behaves ohmically, with a conductance of 20 picosiemens, and the membrane sits at minus 40 millivolts. The difference is 49.1 millivolts, so the current is 0.98 picoamps outward, about 6.1 million ions per second. A carrier cycling hundreds or a few thousand times per second could not carry that. Rate is one way to tell a channel from a carrier.
scenes.visual: Ruler with Vm at -40 and the 49.1 mV gap; a single-channel trace steps to 0.98 pA; the arithmetic; then a log-scale bar chart of ions per second for channel versus carrier.

scenes.tts: Here is the rule: find the equilibrium potential from the concentrations, keeping the sign of the charge. For a cation, a voltage less negative than the equilibrium potential sends net flow outward. A more negative voltage sends it inward. For an anion, the rule flips. Compare the membrane voltage with the equilibrium potential, and you know which way net passive flow goes.
